entities.name: De Re Militari (Epitoma Rei Militaris)
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
Written by Publius Flavius Vegetius Renatus in the late 4th century CE (possibly for Emperor Valentinian II or Theodosius I), the Epitoma Rei Militaris is the single most influential military treatise in Western history. In five books, Vegetius systematically covers: the selection and training of soldiers; legion organization and discipline; battle tactics and formations; siege warfare and fortification; and naval warfare.

Vegetius laments the decline of Roman military standards and advocates a return to the rigorous training and discipline of the early Republic. The work's enduring power lies in its comprehensive, practical approach and its memorable maxims: "Igitur qui desiderat pacem, praeparet bellum" ("Therefore let him who desires peace prepare for war") — one of the most quoted phrases in military history.

Copied in over 200 medieval manuscripts, De Re Militari was the standard military reference for Charlemagne, the Crusaders, English kings, and Renaissance princes, and continued to be cited through the Napoleonic Wars.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Epitoma Rei Militaris had a profound impact on Western military strategy and tactics, influencing leaders such as Napoleon Bonaparte and shaping the course of European warfare for centuries. Its enduring relevance is a testament to Vegetius' comprehensive and practical approach.
